narrative:
The model estimates a 51% chance that you will leave your job, which is just over the threshold for predicting departure. Because of this, the company has decided not to offer you the promotion at this time.

Three factors shaped this outlook more than anything else. First, your total years of experience across all jobs (1–5 years) was the strongest influence, pulling the prediction toward staying rather than leaving. Most employees the model expects to stay also fall in this early-career range, so the system sees your limited overall experience as a reason you are likely to remain. 

The second most important factor worked in the opposite direction: you have received other job offers while working here. Having outside opportunities clearly pushes the prediction toward leaving, as people in similar situations often choose to move on.

Third, your high emotional commitment to the organization pulled the prediction back toward staying. You feel a strong psychological tie to the company, something the model associates with employees who tend to remain.

Taken together, your solid loyalty and modest experience suggest stability, but the presence of external offers creates enough uncertainty that the system expects you may depart. 

The organization should discuss your career goals openly with you and explore whether those external opportunities can be matched internally. You, in turn, may want to reflect on how strongly you wish to stay and grow within this medical-sector role. Addressing these points now could change the outlook for future promotion decisions.
